page.title: C
page.desc: Dennis Ritchie's language from Bell Labs (1972), in which Unix was rewritten in 1973; manual memory management, pointers, and a standard (C89 through C23) that leaves much behaviour undefined on purpose.
page.intro: Dennis Ritchie's language from Bell Labs (1972), in which Unix was rewritten in 1973; manual memory management, pointers, and a standard (C89 through C23) that leaves much behaviour undefined on purpose.

synapses.text: C grew out of B and BCPL so that Unix could be portable; the 1978 Kernighan and Ritchie book defined the language for a generation.
ANSI C (1989) was followed by C99, C11, C17 and C23, each adding features while keeping old code compiling.
C exposes memory directly: arrays decay to pointers, structs have layouts, and malloc/free are your responsibility.
Almost every language can call C, so C headers are how libraries and operating systems talk to each other.

children.title: Pointers and memory
children.desc: A pointer is a variable holding an address. Pointer arithmetic, null, dangling pointers and buffer overruns are where C's power and its security record both come from.

children.title: Undefined behaviour
children.desc: Operations the C standard deliberately leaves unspecified (signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, data races). Compilers may assume they never happen, which enables optimisation and produces surprising code.
